1: On the field of dharma, the field of the Kurus, my own men and the sons of Pāṇḍu gathered, eager to fight. What did they do, Sañjaya?
2: But King Duryodhana, seeing the army of the sons of Pāṇḍu drawn up for battle, then went up to his teacher and spoke.
3: Teacher, look at this great army of the sons of Pāṇḍu, drawn up by your wise pupil, the son of Drupada.
4: Here are heroes, great archers, the equals of Bhīma and Arjuna in battle: Yuyudhāna, Virāṭa and Drupada, the great chariot-warrior.
5: Here are Dhṛṣṭaketu, Cekitāna and the valiant king of Kāśi, and Purujit, Kuntibhoja and Śaibya, a bull among men.
6: Here are the bold Yudhāmanyu and the valiant Uttamaujas, the son of Subhadrā and the sons of Draupadī. Every one of them is a great chariot-warrior.
7: But now, best of the twice-born, know the distinguished men on our side. They are the leaders of my army, and I name them so that you may recognise them.
8: There is your honoured self, and Bhīṣma, Karṇa and Kṛpa, victorious in battle. There is Aśvatthāman and Vikarṇa, and the son of Somadatta as well.
9: And there are many other heroes who have given up their lives for my sake. They carry weapons of many kinds to strike with, and all are skilled in war.
10: That force of ours, guarded by Bhīṣma, is not enough. But this force of theirs, guarded by Bhīma, is enough.
11: And so let all of you, each stationed at your allotted post in every line of advance, be sure to guard Bhīṣma and him alone.
12: Bringing joy to Duryodhana, the mighty grandfather, eldest of the Kurus, gave a loud lion's roar and blew his conch.
13: Then conches and kettledrums, tabors, drums and cow-horns were all sounded at once, and the noise became tumultuous.
14: Then the descendant of Madhu and the son of Pāṇḍu, standing in their great chariot yoked with white horses, blew their two divine conches as well.
15: The lord of the senses blew Pāñcajanya, and the winner of wealth blew Devadatta. The wolf-bellied one, whose deeds are terrible, blew the great conch Pauṇḍra.
16: King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, blew Anantavijaya, and Nakula and Sahadeva blew Sughoṣa and Maṇipuṣpaka.
17: The king of Kāśi, the supreme archer, and Śikhaṇḍin, the great chariot-warrior, joined in, and so did Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Virāṭa and the unconquered Sātyaki.
18: So did Drupada and the sons of Draupadī, and the mighty-armed son of Subhadrā. On every side, lord of the earth, they blew their conches, each his own.
19: That tumultuous noise tore the hearts of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra apart, and it made the sky and the earth resound.
20: Then the son of Pāṇḍu, whose banner bears the monkey, saw the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra drawn up against him. The clash of weapons had begun, and he raised his bow.
21: Then, lord of the earth, he said this to the lord of the senses: place my chariot between the two armies, unfallen one.
22: Hold it there while I look at these men who stand here wanting to fight, and see whom I must fight in this battle we are taking up.
23: Let me look at those who are about to fight, these men who have gathered here wishing to please in war the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, whose buddhi is bad.
24: Descendant of Bharata, when the thick-haired one had spoken to him so, the lord of the senses placed that best of chariots between the two armies.
25: In front of Bhīṣma and Droṇa and all the rulers of the earth, he said: son of Pṛthā, see these Kurus gathered here.
26: There the son of Pṛthā saw fathers and grandfathers standing, and teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons and friends as well.
27: He saw fathers-in-law and well-wishers too, in both of the armies. The son of Kuntī looked closely at all these relatives standing there.
28: Filled with the deepest compassion and despairing, he said this: Kṛṣṇa, I see my own people here, come close and wanting to fight.
29: My limbs give way and my mouth dries up. My body trembles and my hair stands on end.
30: The bow Gāṇḍīva slips from my hand, and my skin burns all over. I cannot stay on my feet, and my mind seems to whirl.
31: And I see omens of ill, Keśava. Nor do I foresee any good in killing my own people in battle.
32: I do not want victory, Kṛṣṇa, nor a kingdom, nor pleasures. What use is a kingdom to us, Govinda? What use are enjoyments, or life?
33: Those for whose sake we want a kingdom, enjoyments and pleasures are the very ones standing here in battle, having given up their lives and their riches.
34: They are teachers, fathers and sons, and grandfathers too. They are maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law and kinsmen by marriage as well.
35: I do not wish to kill them, slayer of Madhu, even though they are killing, not even for kingship over the three worlds. How much less, then, for the sake of the earth?
36: What joy would we have, Janārdana, from striking down the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra? Only evil would settle on us if we killed these aggressors.
37: So we have no right to kill the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, our own relatives. For how could we be happy, Mādhava, after killing our own people?
38: It may be that these men, their minds struck down by greed, do not see the wrong done in destroying the family, or the crime in betraying friends.
39: But how can we not know to turn back from this evil, Janārdana, we who see clearly the wrong done in destroying the family?
40: When the family is destroyed, the eternal family dharmas perish. And when dharma is lost, the opposite of dharma overpowers the whole family.
41: When the opposite of dharma overpowers it, Kṛṣṇa, the women of the family are corrupted. And when the women are corrupted, descendant of Vṛṣṇi, the classes become mixed.
42: That mixing leads only to hell, for the destroyers of the family and for the family. For their ancestors fall, cut off from the rites of rice-ball and water.
43: By these wrongs of the destroyers of the family, which cause the mixing of the classes, the dharmas of the birth-group and the everlasting family dharmas are uprooted.
44: People whose family dharmas are uprooted, Janārdana, are certain to dwell in hell. So we have heard.
45: Ah, alas, what a great evil we are resolved to do: out of greed for the pleasures of a kingdom, we are ready to kill our own people.
46: If the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, weapons in hand, were to kill me in battle, unresisting and unarmed, that would be better for me.
47: Having said this on the battlefield, Arjuna sat down on the seat of his chariot. He cast aside his bow and arrow, his mind shaken by grief.
